title: RAII and smart pointers
goal: Separate ownership from observation and check early-exit cleanup and a weak back-reference.

prerequisites.text: Modules 1–4: input, functions, sequences, ownership, testing and multifile builds.

sections.title: A resource is more than memory
paragraphs: A resource may be memory, a file, a lock or a registered action. Each has acquisition and release operations. Manual cleanup at the bottom of a function is fragile because an early return introduces an easily missed path. RAII connects ownership to an object's lifetime and makes cleanup follow scope exit.

The teaching Resource increments an external counter and decrements it in its destructor. std::make_unique creates an owner whose destructor deletes Resource. When work returns early, the local unique_ptr is still destroyed. This demonstrates ordinary early exit; cleanup during exception propagation is checked separately in the exception lesson.

sections.title: Exclusive ownership
paragraphs: unique_ptr<T> represents the sole owner of a dynamically allocated T. It cannot be copied, but ownership can be transferred by moving. make_unique<T>(args) constructs an object and immediately places it under an owner. get() returns an observing raw pointer; it neither transfers ownership nor permits the caller to delete it.

Dereferencing *p or using p->member requires a nonnull pointer. After reset the previous object is destroyed and its observers are invalid. Never build another unique_ptr from p.get(): that would create two owners and cause repeated deletion. The negative example rejects copying at compile time, before any execution can occur.

sections.title: Worked model
paragraphs: Separate ownership from observation and check early-exit cleanup and a weak back-reference.
steps: Resource increments the count to one.
Early return destroys the local owner.
After work the count is zero: output 1 0.

sections.title: Observers and borrowing
paragraphs: A T& reference or T* pointer often borrows an object owned elsewhere. Identify the owner and the period during which the observer is valid. Passing Resource& to a function that does not retain it bounds the borrowing to that call. Storing a raw pointer in a longer-lived object requires an additional lifetime contract.

Do not replace every pointer with shared_ptr to create an appearance of safety. Ownership should express an architectural decision rather than copying convenience. When data fits directly in a vector or another object's field, separate allocation may be unnecessary. Start with values and justify the need for a dynamic lifetime.

sections.title: Shared ownership and its cost
paragraphs: shared_ptr supports multiple owners through a shared control block. Copying it increases the owner count, and destroying the last owner releases the object. The control block and counter updates have costs, so this is not a free universal pointer. Ownership accounting does not synchronize access to the pointed-to object's state.

make_shared is usually clearer than combining new and shared_ptr manually. Shared ownership should still answer a domain question: why should several independent components determine this object's lifetime? If the answer is merely easier parameter passing, consider a const reference. use_count is not a reliable protocol for exclusive access in concurrent code.

sections.title: Cycles and weak_ptr
paragraphs: When a parent owns a child through shared_ptr and the child strongly owns the parent, both counts may remain nonzero indefinitely. weak_ptr observes a control block without extending the object's lifetime. A back-reference to the parent is therefore often weak, preserving a clear direction of ownership.

lock() obtains a temporary shared_ptr if the object still exists, or returns an empty one otherwise. Acquire the lock first and use its result within that owner's lifetime. In the example observed is destroyed before root.reset(), so the weak pointer is expired afterwards. Destruction cannot be expected while a local strong owner remains alive.

sections.title: Contract boundary check
paragraphs: Separate ownership from observation and check early-exit cleanup and a weak back-reference.
steps: weak_ptr does not keep root alive.
Temporary observed lives in its own scope.
After root.reset(), expired is true: output 1 1.

sections.title: The rule of zero
paragraphs: Members such as vector, string and unique_ptr release their own resources. A class containing them often needs no user-written destructor or special copy and move functions. This is the rule of zero. It reduces the amount of code that must manually coordinate ownership across ordinary and exceptional paths.

The rule of zero does not promise that every such class is copyable. A unique_ptr member disables implicit copying, whereas string and vector usually provide value semantics. That difference is useful. Select member types with suitable contracts, then check which operations the composed type actually supports. The next lesson organizes copy and move semantics.

sections.title: Laboratory: early exits
paragraphs: With n zero, work creates one owner and returns immediately; the final output must be active 0. With n one, two owners exist and the function prints two before returning, followed by active 0. The counter is declared in main and outlives the owners, making observation after work valid.

Extend the test with another early return after the second acquisition and predict active first. Do not add an exception before studying that separate contract. Document each path: acquired resources, responsible owners and resources left afterwards. These checked paths do not establish the absence of every possible leak in a future application.

sections.title: Reviewing an ownership choice
paragraphs: Draw an object graph with separate owns and observes arrows. Give each arrow a lifetime boundary. If strong ownership forms a cycle, identify who breaks it or replace a justified back-reference with weak_ptr. A weak reference is especially useful when disappearance of the target is an acceptable state.

Check for manual deletion of get(), duplicate owners of one address and dereferencing empty pointers. Compare the design with storing a value directly in a container. A successful design often uses fewer pointers rather than more. You can now examine transferring owners between objects without losing responsibility for cleanup.

options: No; ownership can be transferred by moving.
selfcheck.feedback: Copying would create a second owner of one address, violating exclusive ownership, so copy operations are deleted. Ownership transfer uses a move operation rather than an automatic conversion to shared_ptr.

options: An observing pointer without ownership transfer.
selfcheck.feedback: get exposes the address of the already managed object without creating an owner. The observer is valid only while the object lives; deleting it or creating a second owner violates cleanup responsibility.

options: No; access requires a successful lock.
selfcheck.feedback: weak_ptr does not increase the strong-owner count. A successful lock creates a temporary strong owner for access; after the last strong owner disappears, lock returns an empty pointer.

selfcheck.prompt: Does shared_ptr make the target thread safe?
options: No; target state needs its own synchronization protocol.
Yes; if the pointer is const.
selfcheck.feedback: shared_ptr ownership accounting does not synchronize mutations of the target object. Concurrent target operations need their own protocol; making the pointer const does not add a lock.

selfcheck.prompt: Does every class need a user-defined destructor?
options: No; RAII members often allow the rule of zero.
selfcheck.feedback: Members such as vector and string already perform cleanup and compose the containing type's special operations. An unnecessary destructor adds manual responsibility; a unique_ptr member still does not make the type copyable.

selfcheck.prompt: Remove unnecessary shared ownership from a parameter.
selfcheck.feedback: Next: Value semantics, copying and moving

practice.title: Laboratory: RAII and smart pointers
practice.task: Read exactly n=0 or 1. work creates a unique_ptr<Resource> and returns immediately for zero. For one it creates a second owner and prints active followed by a space. Resource increments active at construction and decrements at destruction. After work print active 0 and a newline. Invalid input: invalid.
criteria: Give every link a lifetime boundary.
lock succeeds before the last owner disappears.
The const reference has a justified lifetime.
Include source, actual results, an independent case and limits of the conclusion.

Open Task and Code Studio: the task stays alongside the editor on desktop or in a phone tab. Save your own code before replacing an example.

terms.definition: Tying resource ownership to the lifetime of an owning object.
Construction that immediately places an object under a unique_ptr.
Observing an object while ownership remains elsewhere.
Shared ownership managed through a common control block.
A nonowning link to an object under shared ownership.
Obtaining a temporary strong owner if the object still exists.
Relying on owning members rather than manual special-member operations.
